title: Needs, Wants and Money
bigQuestion: How do people get the things they need and the things they want?

story.title: Leo's Lemonade Stand
story.kicker: Leo wants a bike. He has one jar, a pitcher of lemonade and a hot Saturday.
paragraphs: Leo sees a red bike in the store window. He wants it. It costs a lot. Leo has two dollars in a jar. His mom says, you can earn more. So Leo makes a plan.
On Saturday, Leo sets up a table by the sidewalk. He makes lemonade. He makes a sign. Fifty cents a cup. The sun is hot. Neighbors stop by. Ms. Kim buys a cup. Mr. Bell buys two. The jar gets heavy.
At the end of the day, Leo counts. He has eleven dollars. He is thirsty and tired. He walks past the ice cream truck. He wants a cone. A cone costs two dollars.
Leo stops. If he buys the cone, the bike is farther away. If he saves, the bike is closer. He thinks hard. He puts the money back in the jar. The bike can wait, but not for long.
story.think: Leo had to choose: the cone now or the bike later. What would you choose? Why?

lessons.title: Things We Must Have
lessons.mainIdea: A need is something you must have to live, like food, water, shelter and clothes.
reading: Some things you must have. You must have food. You must have water. You must have a place to sleep. You must have clothes. These are *needs*.
A need is something you cannot live without. Without food, you get weak. Without water, you get sick. Without a home, you get cold and wet. A home is *shelter*.
Think about your day. You ate breakfast. You drank water. You put on clothes. You slept in a bed last night. You met your needs. Every person has the same four needs.

words.d: something you must have to live, like food or water
a place that keeps you safe from cold, rain and heat, like a home

look.title: The Rainy Night
look.text: Look at a family on a rainy night. They are inside. The roof keeps them dry. A pot of soup is on the stove. Each person has a warm sweater. There is a glass of water by each plate. Outside, the rain pours.
look.prompt: Find the four needs in the picture: food, water, shelter, clothes.

check.why: You cannot live without water. It is a need. A toy and candy are not.

choices: A place that keeps you safe and dry
check.why: Shelter is a place like a home. It keeps you safe from cold, rain and heat.

check.q: What happens if a person has no food?
check.why: Food is a need. Without it, a person gets weak. That is why it is a need.

lessons.title: Things We Would Like
lessons.mainIdea: A want is something you would like to have but can live without.
reading: Leo wants a bike. He wants an ice cream cone. He can live without both. They are *wants*. A want is something you would like but do not need.
A toy is a want. A treat is a want. A video game is a want. Wants are fun. It is fine to have wants. But needs come first.
Sometimes it is tricky. Shoes are a need. Your feet must stay safe. A second pair with lights that blink? That is a want. You already have shoes.

words.d: something you would like to have but can live without

look.title: Sort the Bag
look.text: Look at a shopping bag. Inside: a loaf of bread, a bottle of water, a bag of gummy bears, a winter coat, a sticker book and a jug of milk. Some of these things keep you alive. Some are just fun.
look.prompt: Which things in the bag are needs? Which are wants?

choices: Something you would like but can live without
Something you must have to live
check.why: A want is something you would like. Leo can live without a bike, so it is a want.
A sticker book is fun but not needed. Bread and a coat are needs.

check.q: You have shoes. Blinking shoes are what?
choices: A need, because feet must be safe
Not a need or a want
A want, because you already have shoes
check.why: Shoes are a need. A second pair with lights is a want. Your feet are already safe.

lessons.title: Working to Earn
lessons.mainIdea: People work at jobs to earn money.
reading: Leo's mom goes to work. She is a nurse. At the end of the week, she gets paid. She *earns* money. To earn means to get money for work you do.
Almost every grown-up works to earn money. The bus driver earns money. The farmer earns money. The librarian earns money. Then they use it to buy what they need.
Leo worked too. He made lemonade. He sold it. He earned eleven dollars. Work first. Then money. That is how earning goes.

words.d: to get money for work you do
the coins and bills people use to buy things

look.title: Leo's Lemonade Day
look.prompt: When did Leo sell the most cups? Why do you think so?

choices: To get money for work you do
To find money on the ground
check.why: To earn is to get money for work. Leo's mom earns money as a nurse.

check.q: How did Leo earn eleven dollars?
choices: His mom gave it to him
He found it in the park
check.why: Leo worked. He made lemonade and sold it. That is earning.
People do work first. Then they get paid. Work first, then money.

lessons.title: Goods and Services
lessons.mainIdea: Money buys goods, which are things, and services, which is work someone does for you.
reading: Money buys two kinds of things. The first kind is *goods*. Goods are things you can hold. A bike is a good. Bread is a good. A cup of lemonade is a good.
The second kind is *services*. A service is work someone does for you. A haircut is a service. A bus ride is a service. A doctor visit is a service. You pay for the work, not a thing.
Leo sold a good. The lemonade was a thing. Leo's mom sells a service. She cares for sick people. Both earn money. Both help others.

words.d: things people make or grow and sell, like bread or a bike
work that someone does for you, like a haircut

look.title: A Trip Downtown
look.text: Look at Leo and his mom on Saturday. They ride the bus. They buy a new pair of shoes. Leo gets a haircut. They buy two apples. On the way home, a man fixes a flat tire on the bus.
look.prompt: Which things they paid for were goods? Which were services?

choices: A thing you can hold, like bread
check.why: Goods are things you can hold. Bread, a bike and lemonade are goods.
A haircut is work someone does for you. You pay for the work, not a thing.

check.q: Leo's mom is a nurse. What does she sell?
check.why: A nurse does work for people. Caring for the sick is a service.

lessons.title: You Cannot Buy It All
lessons.mainIdea: Money runs out, so you must choose what to buy.
reading: Leo has eleven dollars. The bike costs more. The cone costs two dollars. He cannot have the cone and the bike. Money runs out. So Leo must *choose*.
Every person chooses. Your family chooses at the store. Milk or juice? New shoes or a new coat? No one can buy everything. There is never enough money for it all.
When you choose one thing, you give up another. Leo picks the bike. He gives up the cone. That is the cost of his choice. Think before you choose.

words.d: to pick one thing instead of another

look.title: Three Dollars
look.text: Look at Mia at the school fair. She has three dollars. A popcorn costs two dollars. A ring toss costs two dollars. A sticker costs one dollar. She can buy popcorn and a sticker. Or she can play ring toss and get a sticker. She cannot do all three.
look.prompt: What would you pick? What would you give up?

check.why: Leo has eleven dollars. He cannot buy both the cone and the bike.

check.q: Leo picks the bike. What does he give up?
check.why: When you choose one thing, you give up another. Leo gives up the cone.

check.q: Mia has three dollars. Can she buy all three things?
choices: No, she does not have enough
check.why: All three cost five dollars. Mia has three. She must choose.

lessons.title: Saving Up
lessons.mainIdea: Saving means keeping money now so you can buy something bigger later.
reading: Leo puts his money in the jar. He does not spend it. He is *saving*. To save means to keep money for later. Every dollar in the jar is a step toward the bike.
Saving is hard. You have to wait. The cone is right there. The bike is far away. But each week the jar gets fuller. One day it is enough.
Many people save. A family saves for a car. A grown-up saves for a trip. Some people keep money in a *bank*. A bank keeps money safe until you need it.

words.d: to keep money now so you can use it later
a place that keeps people's money safe

look.title: Leo's Jar, Week by Week
look.cite: Leo's savings chart on the fridge (story)
look.prompt: Does the jar go up or down each week? What is Leo doing?

check.why: To save is to keep money now so you can use it later. Leo saves in a jar.
The cone is right there. The bike is far away. Saving means waiting.
A bank is a place that keeps people's money safe until they need it.

lessons.title: Trading and Sharing
lessons.mainIdea: People can trade or share to get things without using money.
reading: You do not always need money. Sam has two apples. Ana has two cookies. Sam gives Ana an apple. Ana gives Sam a cookie. They *trade*. Each gets something new.
Long ago, most people traded. A farmer traded eggs for shoes. Today we mostly use money. But kids still trade cards. Neighbors still trade help.
You can also *share*. Leo shares his lemonade with his little sister. She pays nothing. Sharing is giving without getting. It makes a community stronger.

words.d: to give one thing and get another thing back
to let someone have or use something of yours

look.title: The Lunch Table
look.text: Look at the lunch table. Sam has grapes. Ana has crackers. Sam gives Ana some grapes. Ana gives Sam some crackers. Jae forgot his lunch. Leo gives Jae half his sandwich. Jae gives nothing back. Leo smiles anyway.
look.prompt: Who traded? Who shared? How can you tell the difference?

choices: Giving one thing and getting another back
check.why: In a trade, each person gives something and gets something. Sam and Ana traded.

check.q: Leo gives Jae half his sandwich. Jae gives nothing back. What is that?
check.why: Sharing is giving without getting anything back. Leo shared.

check.q: Long ago, how did a farmer get shoes?
check.why: Long ago, most people traded. A farmer could trade eggs for shoes.

lessons.title: Farm to Store to Table
lessons.mainIdea: Food starts on a farm, travels to a store, and ends up on your table.
reading: Look at the milk on your table. Where did it come from? Not the store. The store is just one stop. Milk starts on a *farm*. A cow makes it. A farmer milks the cow.
Next a truck picks up the milk. It goes to a place that puts it in jugs. Another truck takes the jugs to the store. A worker puts them on a shelf.
Your family buys the milk. You bring it home. You pour it on your cereal. Farm, truck, store, table. Many workers helped. Each one earned money. Each one did a job.

words.d: a place where people grow food or raise animals

look.title: The Trip of a Corn Flake
look.text: Look at a field in Illinois. Corn grows tall. A farmer picks it with a big machine. A truck takes it to a factory. The factory makes flakes and puts them in a box. A truck takes the box to the store. Your family buys it. You eat it for breakfast.
look.prompt: Count the stops from field to bowl. Who did a job at each stop?

check.why: Milk starts on a farm. A cow makes it and a farmer milks the cow.

check.q: What carries milk from the farm to the store?
check.why: Trucks carry the milk to be put in jugs and then to the store.

check.q: How many workers help get milk to your table?
check.why: The farmer, the truck drivers and the store worker all did a job.

lessons.title: Food Is Work Too
lessons.mainIdea: Growing food is a job, and the food we buy pays the people who grew it.
reading: A farmer in Illinois plants corn in spring. All summer she waters and weeds. In fall she picks it. That is months of work. Then she sells the corn.
Your family pays for food at the store. Some of that money goes to the farmer. Some goes to the truck driver. Some goes to the store worker. Buying food pays for their work.
Not all food comes from a farm. Some people grow tomatoes in a garden. Some catch fish in Lake Michigan. But most food takes many hands. Every meal is a gift of work.

words.d: a plant a farmer grows to sell, like corn or beans

look.title: The Farmer's Year
look.text: Look at the same field four times. Spring: the farmer drives a planter. Brown dirt in rows. Summer: green corn taller than a kid. Fall: a big machine cuts the corn. Winter: the field is white with snow. The farmer fixes her machines in the barn.
look.prompt: When is the farmer working? Is there a season with no work?

choices: A plant a farmer grows to sell
check.why: A crop is a plant grown to sell. Corn is a big crop in Illinois.

check.q: Your family buys corn. Who gets some of that money?
choices: The farmer, the driver and the store worker
check.why: Buying food pays for the work of everyone who helped, not just the store.

check.q: Which season shows the farmer picking corn?
check.why: The farmer plants in spring and picks the corn in fall.

review.why: Food is a need. You cannot live without it. A bike and a sticker are wants.

review.q: How do most grown-ups get money?
review.why: People work at jobs. Then they get paid. That is earning.
A bus ride is work someone does for you. That is a service.

review.q: Leo keeps his money in a jar for the bike. What is he doing?
review.why: Saving means keeping money now to use later. Leo is saving for the bike.

review.q: Why can't Leo buy the cone and the bike?
choices: Money runs out, so he must choose
He does not like ice cream
review.why: No one can buy everything. Leo must choose one and give up the other.
Food starts on a farm. Then it travels by truck to the store and to your table.
